note:
Often a technical term for a prophecy of judgment against a foreign nation (Is. 13:1; 15:1; Nah. 1:1; cf. Mal. 1:1 note).

**Habakkuk the prophet.** See Introduction: Title and Author.

**saw.** The divine message took the form of a supernatural revelation to the prophet’s inner consciousness with no less clarity or vividness than physical sight or hearing (Mic. 1:1).

Habakkuk’s first complaint: The prophet is grieved and shocked by how the wicked prosper at the expense of the righteous. The wicked in the covenant community no longer live like a chosen and saved people (Ex. 19:4–6). But Habakkuk is even more concerned about the Lord’s apparent inactivity. Breach of the covenant is supposed to bring curses and judgment (Deut. 28:15–68). He therefore appeals to the Lord in language reminiscent of the psalms of individual complaint to redress a seemingly hopeless situation. Habakkuk’s passionate dialogue and anguished wrestling with the Lord dominate the first part of the book (1:2–2:20).

**1:2 how long.** This impatient question, characteristic of the psalms of lament (Pss. 13:2; 62:3; Jer. 47:6), indicates both importunity and perseverance in the prophet’s appeal to the Lord, the final judge in matters of covenant disobedience.

**shall I cry.** This indicates the loud cry of someone in deep distress (Pss. 22:24; 30:2).

**Violence.** This term summarizes the deliberate, brutal, and insensitive infringement of the rights and privileges of members of the covenant community. “Destruction” (v. 3) is concerned more with damage to property than malicious personal assault.

**you will not save.** Habakkuk painfully observes the Lord’s seeming indifference and inactivity in the face of undeserved suffering.

The question continues the complaint (cf. Lam. 5:20).

**iniquity.** Lit. “labor” or “toil” that leads to distress, exhaustion, and despondency.

**strife and contention.** Unchecked wickedness results in a divided community riddled with suspicions, accusations, and personal attacks.

Lit. “the law is numb.” The word for “law” (Hb. _torah_) denotes the divinely revealed standard for covenant life. The power and influence of the wicked have rendered the law ineffectual because just judges cannot be found. Even so, there is still a righteous remnant in the land.

**the wicked.** Those in Israel who spurn the Lord’s will and law. They dominate society in Judah, preventing the righteous from receiving justice.

**1:5–11** God’s first response: The Lord is already at work. He will send the Babylonians to judge His people. He uses strange instruments against His unfaithful people—the terrifying Babylonians (cf. Is. 10:5, 6).

At the time of Habakkuk’s complaint to God, the Babylonians have not yet come to a position of power in the ancient Near East. Everyone will be surprised by the coming of the Babylonians to punish the wicked in Judah.

The sovereign God of Israel controls every power in history, including the aggressive Chaldeans.

**Chaldeans.** Also called Babylonians, or Neo-Babylonians, the Chaldeans took control in Babylon in 626 B.C. as the power of Assyria declined. They played a key role in the destruction of Nineveh, capital of Assyria, in 612 B.C. After routing the Egyptian army in 605 B.C., they established an empire that lasted until the Persians captured the capital city of Babylon in 539 B.C.
This describes the arrogance of the coming enemy whose standards of action and honor are entirely self-determined and self-centered, with no respect for the rights of others, let alone God.

Vivid images portray the speed and resolution of these fierce and overpowering warriors.

**evening wolves.** Ravenous because they have not eaten all day, and therefore ferocious and unflinching in identifying and devouring prey.

The intimidating Babylonian armies look at obstacles as challenges and treat their opposition with contempt.

**pile up earth.** Siege ramps built by attackers to gain access to a fortified city’s walls.

verse_quote: whose own might is their god.
note: Or “this his power is his god.” Pride, especially the deification of one’s own power, is offensive to God, who alone deserves our worship.

Habakkuk’s second complaint: We do not know what length of time has elapsed between Habakkuk’s complaints. He expresses his perplexity at the Lord’s plan to use the wicked Babylonians to punish Israel because it seems to be in flagrant opposition to God’s own revealed character.

**1:12 from everlasting.** As the eternal God of history and Lord of His people, He is free to choose the agents of chastisement. In faith, Habakkuk begins by setting out what he is sure of—God’s character.

**my God, my Holy One.** A personal relationship to the incomparable God, the Holy One, turns confusion into conviction that the present anguish will not be the end.

**We shall not die.** This voices faith’s confidence that the Lord will fulfill His covenant commitment to Israel (Jer. 31:36; 33:23–26).

**O Rock.** This ancient Mosaic name for God emphasizes divine dependability and protection (Deut. 32:4 note).

How can the holy and all-powerful God, to whom sin is totally repugnant, permit evil to go unchecked and unpunished?

**traitors.** Lit. “those acting treacherously.” The reference is to the Babylonians. Habakkuk cannot fathom how the holy God can use such an unscrupulous and wicked nation to punish Judah, whose conduct is by comparison “more righteous.”

A bold accusation by Habakkuk. If the Lord tolerates the evil actions of the Babylonians, He becomes responsible for the fate of their victims.

**like the fish.** Imagery of Babylon as a fisherman catching helpless fish is developed in vv. 14–17. Fishing was an important activity in Babylonia, which was located in the region of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and was bordered on the south by the Persian Gulf. Some ancient Near Eastern wall reliefs portray victorious rulers carrying captives in fishnets.

**no ruler.** There is no one to protect them. Kings in the ancient Near East were seen as the protectors of their people (1 Sam. 8:20). An implicit accusation may also be present here, since the Lord is the ultimate king and protector of His people (Deut. 33:5; Is. 63:18, 19).
The instruments of their success are idolized and worshiped (v. 11 note).

God’s second response:Habakkuk receives an answer to his painful questions of 1:12–17. God will show that He is just and the justifier of those who have faith in Him. The final outcome of history will be worship of the one holy and just king (v. 20). The destiny of nations and individuals alike will be determined by their attitude toward God as expressed in persevering and faithful dependence or haughty rejection (Pss. 1; 2:2, 3). In the meantime, God calls on His people to live through persevering faith.

**2:1** A transitional verse. Habakkuk’s anguished questioning drives him to the fount of all wisdom to wait for an answer. His words express his determination to wait for an answer. God is sovereign in word as well as in deed—His revelation cannot be forced.

**watchpost ... tower.** Military terms figuratively depict the prophet as a watchman on the lookout for a word from God (Is. 62:6, 7; Ezek. 3:16; 33:1–9).

In order that it might be preserved and transmitted (cf. Jer. 30:2; Nah. 1:1) as a long-term witness because the Lord’s intervention will take time to develop.

**vision.** See note on 1:1.

**so he may run who reads it.** Perhaps a figure (though some suggest that Habakkuk actually writes an oracle on large tablets) indicating that Habakkuk’s prophecy is to be publicized. Either the writing is to be so clear that a courier who is running with the tables can read them, or that its clarity will enable passersby to read without difficulty (i.e., “that one may read it swiftly”).

A fixed period must elapse before the prophecy will be fulfilled, but this should not be regarded as failure or deception. Rather, this time can be endured with the Lord’s guarantee of approaching fulfillment. Judgment on the Babylonians came (long after Habakkuk’s vision) through Cyrus on October 29, 539 B.C.

The Lord here discloses the essential distinction He makes between the wicked, the Babylonians, and the righteous, the remnant of Judah. The wicked take paths that lead to death and defeat; the righteous by faith take a path that leads to life and victory. His distinction and the promise it contains for the righteous bring a word of comfort to Habakkuk. It also marks the turning point in his personal struggle over the Lord’s use of the wicked Babylonians as a rod of judgment against His people.

**puffed up.** The Babylonian king and kingdom, the embodiment of wickedness in the world. Habakkuk earlier described their arrogance (1:7, 10, 11).

**by his faith.** Or “by his faithfulness.” In context here, the Hb. word denotes steadfast reliance on the Lord, a trust that perseveres. In the midst of a land filled with wickedness (1:2–4) and subject to the wrath of God, the Lord promises that a righteous remnant in Judah will trust in the God who remembers mercy in His wrath (3:2). The Hebrew recalls the words of Gen. 15:6 and applies them to Habakkuk’s situation. By faith, Abraham waited patiently for the fulfillment of God’s promises (Heb. 6:15), and now Habakkuk and the remnant must wait patiently as well (v. 3; 3:16). Here Paul finds scriptural proof for the doctrine of justification by faith (Rom. 1:17; Gal. 3:11), and Habakkuk’s word of comfort has been a key text for Protestant faith since the sixteenth century.

verse_quote: wine is a traitor ... arrogant man.
note:
The arrogance and insatiability of the Babylonians is compared to a drunkard besotted with wine.

**Sheol ... death.** It is proverbial in Habakkuk’s day that death is like a devouring mouth always ready for more to die (Prov. 1:12; 27:20; 30:15, 16).

This section of woes forms a distinct literary unit. Prophetic judgments are presented here in a taunt song, a poetic form that mocks the defeated.

**2:6–8** The first woe. Those who plunder others will themselves be plundered.

**2:6 all these.** Judah and all those who have suffered under the Babylonian oppressor. The prophecies of woe in vv. 6–20 are depicted in such general and proverbial terms that they acquire a universal applicability to the struggle of the persecuted righteous against the wicked.

**Woe.** The Hebrew word is apparently an interjection derived from the funeral lament (sometimes rendered “Alas”; cf. 1 Kin. 13:30), but is often used in prophecies of judgment.

**pledges.** The heavy tribute exacted by the Bab­ylonians is figuratively depicted as articles taken in security for debts.
The violence and bloodshed through which the Babylonians have gained their plunder cries out to be avenged (v. 11; cf. Gen. 4:10).

The second woe condemns those who seek security and economic gain at the expense of others.

**2:9 nest on high.** Birds of prey often make their nests in high and inaccessible places. Likewise, the Babylonians consider their position in world history to be secure (Is. 14:13, 14; 47:7).

A striking personification. This cry against injustice will emerge from building materials stolen from others or purchased with unjust gain.

**2:12–14** The third woe pronounces judgment on the ruthless but futile efforts of the tyrant to perpetuate his fame.

Babylonian inscriptions confirm the high premium placed on building activities. Nebuchadnezzar, who used subjugated peoples as forced laborers, took special pride in his building of Babylon (Dan. 4:30). Such projects involved loss of life and were paid for with the spoils of war.

**... nothing.** God sovereignly ensures that the efforts of the proud to perpetuate their own glory amount to nothing. Instead, the “earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord” (v. 14).
No longer merely the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34, 35) or the temple (1 Kin. 8:11), but the whole earth will acknowledge divine glory.
The fourth woe pronounces judgment on Babylon’s sadistic and humiliating treatment of others.
**’s right hand.** This biblical metaphor indicates divine retribution (Is. 51:17–23). What the Babylonians have done to others will be done to them (vv. 7, 8).

Military campaigns usually caused extensive damage to plants and animals. Trees supplied building materi­al and firewood (Deut. 20:19, 20); wild and domestic animals were killed for food. Many cedar trees were lost during the Babylonian campaign against Lebanon (Is. 14:8). God’s concern for His creation should be noted.
The fifth woe denounces idolatry, the worship of false gods, as futile and foolish (Is. 44:9–17; 57:12, 13).

Lit. “palace,” the heavenly sanctuary from which the Lord, the Great King, rules His world (Ps. 11:4).

**let all the earth keep silence.** A sharp contrast is drawn between the silent idols (v. 19) and the living God, before whom all others must keep silence. The woes of judgment on the proud and wicked culminate in the universal silence of worship in the glorious presence of the incomparable God (v. 14; Ps. 46:10).

This chapter records the persevering prayer of Habakkuk. In moving hymnic style, Habakkuk responds (vv. 16–19) to the Lord’s revelation (2:2–5) of His imminent intervention in history on behalf of His people (vv. 3–15). As the Babylonians represent the proud and wicked on their way to ruin, Habakkuk now exemplifies the righteous faithful persevering and already rejoicing in hope of the Lord’s promise of life.

**3:1 prayer.** Here perhaps a synonym for hymn (Ps. 72:20). The musical and liturgical notations in the heading, text, and conclusion of this prayer are like those commonly found in the psalms. See Introduction to Psalms: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

The invocation or prologue to the hymn.

**heard the report.** Habakkuk’s patience in standing before the Lord (2:1 note) is rewarded by a vision based on God’s mighty deeds in the past.

**revive it.** Habakkuk’s prayer is that the Lord would be as present and active as He was in the time of Moses.

**in wrath remember mercy.** A prayer for the gracious combination of divine judgment tempered by mercy.

Habakkuk’s prayer portrays a theophany, or visible self-manifestation of God, using imagery found in the traditional descriptions of God’s appearances at the exodus from Egypt, at the giving of the covenant law at Sinai, and during the conquest of Canaan (Ex. 15:1–18; Deut. 33:2, 3; Judg. 5:4, 5; Pss. 18:10; 68:7, 8, 24; 77:16–20).

**3:3 Teman.** The name of Esau’s grandson represents the land of Edom (Amos 1:12 note).

**Mount Paran.** A mountain in the wilderness of the Sinai peninsula (Deut. 33:2). The imagery of vv. 3–7 is that of God’s march to His holy mountain and, subsequently, His act of leading His people to take possession of the land He had won for them.
Habakkuk pictures ominous dimensions of God’s coming in judgment (Deut. 28:21, 22).
These are possibly alternative names for one people or area, perhaps for nomads from the Sinai peninsula.

The prophet here directly addresses God. The approaching Lord is the invincible divine warrior who demonstrates His lordship over the cosmos. Similar poetic imagery is known from Canaanite and other mythologies.

**3:8 rivers …** **sea.** The Lord has demonstrated His power over the river Nile (Ex. 7:14–24), the Jordan (Josh. 3:14–17), and the Red Sea (Ex. 14:21–30).
See Josh. 10:12, 13.

The Lord of nature also has absolute power over the forces of history. He comes to deliver His people and judge the wicked.

**3:12 threshed.** An agricultural image derived from the way grain was threshed by violent beating or trampling (Amos 1:3 note).

In the past the Lord came out of His sanctuary for the salvation of His people in distress. This is what Habakkuk is expecting Him to do again.

**for the salvation ... anointed.** Or, “to save Your Anointed.” Perhaps a synonym for the chosen people of Israel (cf. Ps. 105:15), but more probably a reference to the Davidic kingship as it comes to final expression in the Messiah (Ps. 132:10).
Habakkuk refers again to the exodus history in which God displayed His undisputed dominion over natural and historical forces.

Together with v. 2, this verse encloses the hymn of vv. 3–15 with autobiographical references at beginning and end.

**my body trembles.** Habakkuk describes in physical terms the profound effect that the divine self-revelation has had on him (cf. Jer. 4:19). The Lord has answered his painful questions and will hear his prayer.

**I will quietly wait ... of trouble.** Awed by the divine majesty, Habakkuk can rest in the assurance that the Lord will judge the wicked.

Even when crops and herds fail (a horrifying thought in the context of an agricultural economy), and society lives with hunger and poverty, Habakkuk’s trusting expectation will not be crushed. Hope and trust transform his fear of the future into the desire to rejoice always in God his Savior (Rom. 8:35–39)., 18

verse_quote: GOD, the Lord, is my strength.
note:
Total dependence on the sovereign covenant Lord is Habakkuk’s key to life.

**feet like the deer’s ... tread on my high places.** This striking figure portrays the strength and confidence that the Lord imparts to the righteous (Is. 40:29–31).

**choirmaster.** See note on v. 1.
